findings.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection below target; cost-of-living distress and court enforcement delays threaten further deterioration
findings.detail: Council Tax achieved 27.50% collection against profiled target of 27.70% (0.20% shortfall); Business Rates achieved 26.53% against 26.43% target. Material underlying pressures: cost-of-living creating significant financial distress for residents and businesses, and HM Court unable to provide regular enforcement dates. These factors suggest collection challenges may persist or worsen.
findings.matters: Collection rates below target reduce available cash and may require bad debt provision increases. Court enforcement constraints coupled with cost-of-living pressures indicate collection challenges may be structural rather than temporary.
findings.figures: Council Tax: 27.50% vs 27.70% profiled target; Business Rates: 26.53% vs 26.43% target
findings.quote: Whilst the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) were rebased for 2026/27, the in-year collection remains challenging. The ongoing cost of living challenge is resulting in significant financial distress for large numbers of customers, making payment of increased Council tax demands problematic. HM Court service are also unable to provide regular court dates to support smooth enforcement.

findings.headline: HRA tenant rent arrears deteriorating: up to 1.49% of annual rental income from 1.15% year-on-year
findings.detail: Rent arrears increased by 0.34 percentage points. While the council incorporates bad debt provision and monitors arrears tightly, the upward trend reflects cost-of-living pressures on tenants. Continued deterioration could require higher bad debt provisions and further strain HRA finances.
findings.matters: Deteriorating rent collection indicates tenant financial stress and reduces reliable HRA income. This compounds existing deficits and could necessitate higher bad debt provisions, further pressuring service sustainability.
findings.figures: HRA rent arrears: 1.15% (prior year) → 1.49% (current), increase of 0.34 percentage points
findings.quote: Current tenant rent arrears rose from 1.15% to 1.49% of annual rental income over the past year.

findings.headline: HRA stock condition survey (91.5% complete) may identify additional capital investment requirements above budget
findings.detail: The housing stock condition survey remains 91.5% incomplete. The council acknowledges completion may result in additional capital spend beyond current budget. Given the HRA is already running a £456k deficit, any material findings would create further pressure on constrained finances.
findings.matters: Unquantified cost pressures emerging on a service already running deficits represents material financial uncertainty. Completion of this survey could reveal substantial additional needs, further straining finances.
findings.figures: Survey 91.5% complete; no estimate provided for potential additional spend
findings.quote: The stock condition survey is 91.5% complete which may result in additional spend being required above the current level of investment included in the budget.

findings.headline: Supported housing cost gap creating increasing pressures on General Fund with no quantified solution identified
findings.detail: The council identifies a structural cost gap: the difference between actual cost to provide supported housing (via charities and private sector) and recoverable housing benefit creates increasing General Fund pressure. The scale of this gap is unquantified and no mitigation strategy is articulated beyond acknowledging the pressure.
findings.matters: This is a non-discretionary service cost for a rising demand (homelessness). The unquantified financial gap with no identified solution represents open-ended exposure that could grow and impact General Fund sustainability.
findings.figures: No figures provided for scale of gap or solution
findings.quote: the gap between the cost to the Council of the supported housing premium (when the housing is provided by charities and the private sector) and the lower level of housing benefit that can be reclaimed is creating increasing pressures on the GF.

findings.headline: Capital resources are depleted and cannot be easily replaced from revenue or future capital receipts
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that capital resources (excluding borrowing) are now depleted and cannot be easily replaced. This constraint is particularly acute given the concurrent £500k reduction in Right-to-Buy receipts. All future capital investment is now constrained to available borrowing or new revenue-generated funding.
findings.matters: Depleted capital resources constrain the council's ability to maintain assets, fund regeneration, or respond to infrastructure needs without increased borrowing. This is a material strategic constraint on the council's investment flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital receipts reduced by £500k (from £2.2m to £1.7m); capital resources identified as depleted
findings.quote: Capital resources (other than borrowing) are depleted and will not be easily replaced from revenue contributions or capital receipts.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account deficit worsened by £173k in Q1 to £456k, requiring £455k drawdown from reserves
findings.detail: The HRA deficit deteriorated from the budgeted £283k to a £456k projected outturn. The primary driver is the £265k interest cost on Right-to-Buy receipt repayments—a governance failure rather than market condition. This requires a £455k contribution from the Housing Initiatives Reserve to cover the operational deficit.
findings.matters: A worsening deficit driven by delivery failure rather than external factors, in Q1 of the year, raises sustainability concerns. Reliance on reserve drawdowns to fund operational deficits reduces financial flexibility and may signal the HRA cannot achieve balance without further reserve depletion.
findings.figures: HRA deficit: £283k (budget) → £456k (Q1 forecast), adverse variance of £173k; reserve contribution £455k
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account – £173k net adverse variances identified, leading to an increased deficit of £456k forecast for 2026/27.

findings.headline: £505k of historic Right-to-Buy receipts must be repaid to MHCLG due to failure to spend within statutory deadlines; interest charge of £265k
findings.detail: Following audit, the council identified £505k of retained Right-to-Buy receipts allocated to projects from 2021/22 onwards that were not spent within prescribed timescales and must be repaid to MHCLG. Interest at base rate plus 8% (totalling £265k) will be charged and funded from the Housing Initiatives Reserve. This reduces available capital receipts balance from £2.2m to £1.7m, directly reducing capital funding capacity.
findings.matters: This represents both loss of capital resources and a governance failure in project delivery. Failure to deploy capital resources on time indicates weak project management or delivery, a material concern for lenders assessing financial control.
findings.figures: £505k repayment required, £265k interest charge (base rate plus 8%), capital receipts balance reduced from £2.2m to £1.7m
findings.quote: Following a recent review and audit of the receipts allocated to projects dating back to 2021/22 it has been identified that £505k of historic receipts were not spent in the allotted time and will need to be repaid to MHCLG.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream have improved from 15.8% to 10.9%, but are budgeted to rise to 13.5% as HRA borrowing impacts future years
findings.detail: The actual financing cost burden improved significantly from £3.1m (2024/25) to £2.4m (2025/26), despite increased capital expenditure. However, the budget projects financing costs will increase to £2.8m (13.5% of revenue stream) in 2026/27, reflecting the impact of new HRA borrowing beginning to service.
findings.matters: Financing costs as a percentage of revenue stream is a key indicator of financial sustainability for lenders. While currently improving, the trajectory is expected to reverse as new debt servicing costs impact the revenue budget
findings.figures: Financing costs: £3.1m (2024/25), £2.4m (2025/26), £2.8m (2026/27); As proportion of net revenue stream: 15.8%, 10.9%, 13.5% respectively
findings.quote: The net annual charge is known as financing costs; this is compared to the net revenue stream i.e. the amount funded from Council Tax, business rates and general government grants.

findings.headline: General Fund capital expenditure is planned to fall to zero in 2027/28, having been £9.8m in 2026/27 and £18.5m in 2025/26
findings.detail: The General Fund capital programme is projected to end entirely by 2027/28. The council's capital strategy is increasingly focused on HRA housing investment. Current General Fund projects include Dover Beacon (£12.6m) and the Tides Leisure Centre replacement.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether zero General Fund capital spending is planned completion of the current programme or reflects inability to fund ongoing capital renewal needs in services
findings.quote: The main General Fund capital projects to date have included Dover Beacon Project, and major restoration works on Maison Dieu (Dover Town Hall), Tides Leisure Centre replacement, and Deal Pier structural repairs.

findings.headline: Debt is projected to increase from £10.9m to £82.4m between March 2026 and March 2027, driven by capital expenditure financing
findings.detail: The significant increase in debt reflects the HRA capital programme financing strategy. The debt spike is consistent with the Capital Financing Requirement growing from £160.7m to £182.6m over the same period. Current borrowing stands at £118.1m against an Authorised Limit of £338.5m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's debt trajectory and its position relative to legal borrowing limits. The 655% projected increase in debt in a single year represents a major financial commitment that must be serviceable from the council's revenue stream
findings.figures: Debt: £10.9m (31.3.2026), £82.4m (31.3.2027), £40.9m (31.3.2028); Capital Financing Requirement: £160.7m to £182.6m; Current borrowing £118.1m against Authorised Limit £338.5m
findings.quote: Statutory guidance is that debt should remain below the capital financing requirement, except in the short term. The Council has complied and expects to continue to comply with this requirement in the medium term as is shown below.

findings.headline: HRA capital expenditure is planned to increase dramatically to £83.3m in 2026/27, up from £23.9m actual in 2025/26 - a 248% increase
findings.detail: The council is pursuing an ambitious housing development programme. In 2025/26, it delivered 63 additional homes. The HRA Affordable Housing Development Project is budgeted at £21.1m. This represents a major strategic shift in capital allocation toward council housing provision.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council's capital commitments and debt trajectory. A near-tripling of HRA capital spending signals major new borrowing requirements and future repayment obligations that will impact the council's revenue budget
findings.figures: HRA capital expenditure: £23.9m (2025/26 actual) to £83.3m (2026/27 budget); HRA Affordable Housing Development Project £21.1m; 63 homes delivered in 2025/26
findings.quote: HRA capital expenditure is recorded separately. The Council delivered 63 additional homes to our housing stock, including temporary and general needs accommodation. Additional homes are in the pipeline, as part of our ambitious multi-million-pound programme to provide much-needed homes for local people.

findings.headline: Borrowing maturity concentrated in short-term – half of debt due within 12 months
findings.detail: The council holds £59.4m (50.3%) of its £118.1m total borrowing maturing within 12 months, creating material refinancing exposure. Short-term borrowing increased from £37m to £55.5m in the year. Late-year short-term borrowing costs surged to 5-7% from earlier 4-4.5% levels, and this concentration means the council must refinance roughly half its debt in coming months at prevailing market rates.
findings.matters: High concentration of near-term debt maturity creates refinancing risk – if rates remain elevated or market conditions tighten, the council faces forced reissuance of half its debt book at potentially significantly higher cost than its longer-term fixed portfolio
findings.figures: £59.4m of £118.1m total borrowing due within 12 months (50.3%); formal short-term borrowing £55.5m, up £18.5m year-on-year; late-year rates reached 5-7%
findings.quote: At 31st March 2026 the Council held £55.5m of short-term loans, an increase of £18.5m to 31 st March 2025, as part of its strategy for funding previous years' capital programmes.

findings.headline: Forecast borrowing requirement to rise 58% from £74m to £116.9m by 2028
findings.detail: The liability benchmark, which estimates the minimum borrowing the council must hold to fund its capital and revenue plans, is forecast to escalate rapidly. Actual borrowing need at 31 March 2026 was £74.0m; this is forecast to reach £104.9m by 2027 and £116.9m by 2028. This 58% two-year growth trajectory indicates material expansion of capital commitments or emerging revenue pressures ahead.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising forecast borrowing needs suggest the council's spending plans are outpacing revenue generation, raising questions about sustainability and future refinancing capacity – core assessment points for lenders
findings.figures: Liability benchmark forecast: £74.0m actual (31/3/26), £104.9m forecast (31/3/27), £116.9m forecast (31/3/28)
findings.quote: Liability benchmark 58.2 74.0 104.9 116.9

findings.headline: Interest rate risk limit exceeded – council exposed to £693k revenue impact from 1% rate movement, above £500k threshold
findings.detail: Dover's treasury management prudential indicator for interest rate exposure is non-compliant. The council's actual interest rate sensitivity is £693k per 1% movement in rates, against an approved limit of £500k. This 38% overage reflects end-of-year short-term borrowing undertaken at elevated market rates of 5-7%, well above the 4-4.5% rates common earlier in the year.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with approved risk thresholds signals a loss of control over interest rate exposure, a material concern for lenders assessing the council's financial management quality and vulnerability to rate volatility
findings.figures: Actual interest rate exposure £693k vs approved limit £500k per 1% rate move
findings.quote: Upper limit on one-year revenue impact of a 1% rise in interest rates £500k £693k x

findings.paper_title: Annual Write Off Report for Housing Services 2025-26
findings.headline: Bad debt provision for rents increased 17% from £65,359 to £76,559, reflecting elevated arrears risk
findings.detail: The council increased its bad debt provision by £11,200 based on updated arrears analysis. This reflects the council's assessment that collection risk has deteriorated beyond previous expectations given the rising current tenant arrears.
findings.matters: Bad debt provision increases reduce usable HRA reserves and signal the council's assessment that collection recovery has deteriorated materially.
findings.figures: Bad debt provision £76,559 in 2025-26 vs £65,359 in 2024-25 (increase of £11,200)
findings.quote: The bad debt provision for rents in 2024/25 was £65,359. However, this has been increased to £76,559 based on the arrears analysis for bad debt.

findings.paper_title: Annual Write Off Report for Housing Services 2025-26
findings.headline: Current tenant arrears as a percentage of rental income rose from 1.15% to 1.49%, with staffing recruitment difficulties preventing mitigation
findings.detail: Current tenant arrears increased from £293,858 to £398,751. The council identifies two drivers: the cost of living crisis reducing tenants' ability to pay rent, and challenges recruiting specialist benefits advisors who help tenants maximize income to support rent payments.
findings.matters: Rising collection failure indicates weakening HRA financial resilience and tenant vulnerability, with staffing constraints preventing the council from mitigating cost-of-living impacts.
findings.figures: Current tenant arrears as percentage of annual rental income: 1.49% in 2025-26 vs 1.15% in 2024-25; absolute arrears £398,751 vs £293,858
findings.quote: Challenges to recruiting key vacant roles in the team due to the high level of expertise required in benefits and financial support.

findings.paper_title: Annual Write Off Report for Housing Services 2025-26
findings.headline: Housing write-offs rose 18% to £122,954 in 2025-26, attributed to prior-year staff shortages affecting arrears management
findings.detail: Write-offs of £122,954 in 2025-26 exceeded the prior year's £103,801. The council attributes this increase to a period when the income recovery team operated with only two rent officers, limiting their ability to manage tenant arrears proactively before tenancy termination.
findings.matters: Rising write-offs despite modest absolute levels (0.4% of billings) signal operational capacity constraints in income recovery that create ongoing governance and financial risk.
findings.quote: This is higher than the 2024/25 level of £103,801 due to a prolonged period where the team were operating with only two rent officers, which limited our ability to proactively manage and reduce the arrears prior to the termination of tenancies.

findings.headline: Council breached prudential indicator for interest rate risk exposure
findings.detail: Dover exceeded its interest rate risk exposure target in 2025/26. The council's exposure to a 1% interest rate move is £693k, against a £500k prudential target—39% overshoot. The council has revised the 2026/27 target to £750k, indicating the breach reflects how it balanced its £118m borrowing against £55m cash holdings and pooled investments.
findings.matters: Prudential indicators exist to ensure councils manage debt within intended risk tolerances; exceeding the interest rate risk metric signals the debt/investment mix is exposed to more interest rate volatility than the council intended, which affects financial resilience and lender confidence.
findings.figures: Interest rate exposure: £693k; target: £500k; total borrowing: £118m; cash and investments: £55m; revised 2026/27 target: £750k
findings.quote: The Council has operated within the Prudential Indicators in compliance with the Council's Treasury Management Practices on all areas except for the indicator for the Council's exposure to interest rate risk. This shows that were the interest rates increase or decrease by 1% the difference between the interest receivable and payable would be £693k whereas the target for 2025/26 is £500k.

findings.paper_title: DDC - Quarterly Internal Audit Update Report 25-06-2026
findings.headline: Housing Benefit Subsidy claims for 2024/25 and 2025/26 have not yet been assessed by external auditors, creating income uncertainty
findings.detail: The report identifies that Grant Thornton's verification of subsidy claims is significantly behind schedule: 2022/23 claims are currently being signed off, 2023/24 is under review, but claims for 2024/25 and 2025/26 have not yet been assessed. The report flags this as essential to resolve before April 2028 Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.matters: Unverified subsidy claims represent uncertain housing benefit income to the council; delays in verification can result in unexpected financial adjustments and loss of reimbursement.
findings.figures: Claims for 2024/25 and 2025/26 remain unassessed; LGR deadline April 2028
findings.quote: Grant Thornton (External Auditors) are currently in the process of signing off the subsidy claims for 2022/23 at each council. The subsidy claims for 2023/24 are in the process of being reviewed and the claims for 2024/25 and 2025/26 are yet to be assessed. Given the proposed Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) scheduled for April 2028, it is essential to ensure that Grant Thornton are fully up to date with the verification and sign-off of all subsidy claims for each council by that point.

findings.paper_title: DDC - Quarterly Internal Audit Update Report 25-06-2026
findings.headline: Fraud Resilience and Rechargeable Works both have Limited Assurance with follow-up reviews stalled since September 2025 and June 2025 respectively
findings.detail: Fraud Resilience was reported with Limited Assurance in September 2025 and remains work-in-progress; Rechargeable Works has been Limited Assurance since June 2025 and also remains work-in-progress. Neither has a clear completion date for their follow-up reviews.
findings.matters: Unresolved control weaknesses in fraud detection and income-generating processes represent ongoing operational and financial risks to the council.
findings.figures: Fraud Resilience (September 2025, Limited, work-in-progress); Rechargeable Works (June 2025, Limited, work-in-progress)
findings.quote: Fraud Resilience 18-09-2025 Limited Work-in-Progress; Rechargeable Works 26-06-2025 Limited Work-in-Progress

findings.paper_title: DDC - Quarterly Internal Audit Update Report 25-06-2026
findings.headline: Main Accounting System remains with Limited Assurance, indicating unresolved significant control gaps
findings.detail: Reported in September 2025 with Limited Assurance and remains work-in-progress for follow-up review. Limited Assurance means the system has significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance requiring improvement to the governance, risk management and control framework.
findings.matters: The Main Accounting System is fundamental to financial reporting and control; unresolved Limited Assurance indicates the council's ability to produce reliable financial statements remains at risk.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance level assigned; review status remains work-in-progress as of May 31, 2026
findings.quote: Main Accounting System 18-09-2025 Limited Work-in-Progress; Limited assurance - Significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance were identified. Improvement is required to the system of governance, risk management and control to effectively manage risks to the achievement of objectives in the area audited.

findings.headline: Dedicated resource had to be added to resolve bank reconciliation delays
findings.detail: The statement notes that 'Dedicated resource continued to be applied to the bank reconciliation process to work to bring the process up to date during the year.' This was required because Bank Reconciliation initially received a No Assurance audit opinion, indicating the reconciliation process had broken down or was significantly behind.
findings.matters: Bank reconciliation is a basic cash management control; requiring dedicated resource to catch up and initially failing audit suggests cash position visibility was compromised, which is a red flag for financial management.
findings.figures: Bank Reconciliation: No Assurance (initial) → Reasonable (follow-up)
findings.quote: Dedicated resource continued to be applied to the bank reconciliation process to work to bring the process up to date during the year.

findings.headline: Council is aware of S114 notices issued elsewhere in Kent and Medway and treats this as a corporate risk
findings.detail: The risk register explicitly lists R27 'S114 notices issued within Kent and Medway' as a red-level strategic risk affecting the Council's Modernising our Council priority. This indicates the Council is monitoring insolvency/financial distress notices issued to neighbouring councils as a warning indicator for its own sustainability.
findings.matters: A council's explicit acknowledgment that neighbouring councils have reached insolvency thresholds (Section 114 of Local Government Finance Act 1988) and treatment of this as a direct risk to its own operations signals sector-wide financial stress and recognition of contagion risk.
findings.figures: R27 S114 notices issued within Kent and Medway, listed as red risk
findings.quote: R27 S114 notices issued within Kent and Medway

findings.headline: 23 high-severity audit recommendations remain overdue and escalated to governance committee
findings.detail: During 2025/26, 23 agreed management actions from internal audit were escalated to the Governance Committee as they were not implemented at follow-up. Of these: 17 are now implemented, three are partially implemented with revised dates of September 2026 and April 2027, and three remain outstanding with a revised date of December 2026. This represents 5 Critical and 18 High-risk recommendations not completed on time.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-severity audit recommendations indicate delayed implementation of control improvements; a lender would want to know whether critical control gaps have been properly remediated or remain open.
findings.figures: 23 escalated (5 Critical, 18 High); 17 implemented, 3 partially implemented, 3 outstanding
findings.quote: Throughout the 2025/26 year there have been 23 agreed management actions that were escalated to the Governance Committee as they were not implemented at the time of follow up. These have been tracked though to completion through CMT and Heads of Service, 17 are now implemented, three partially implemented and on track for September 2026 and April 2027 and three outstanding with a revised date of December 2026

findings.headline: Internal audit gave only Reasonable (not Substantial) assurance, with explicit caveat that control position continues changing
findings.detail: East Kent Audit Partnership concluded 'Reasonable Assurance' for 2025/26 whilst noting that 'for the period following 31 March 2026... much work has been undertaken, and the position is a continuously moving target.' In the same year, 44% of completed audit reviews received only Limited assurance and 6% received No Assurance.
findings.matters: Reasonable (not Substantial) assurance means the auditor identified significant control deficiencies; the caveat that the position is a 'continuously moving target' signals ongoing remediation work and control instability, which would concern lenders assessing financial management capability.
findings.figures: 5 Substantial, 4 Reasonable, 8 Limited, 1 No Assurance out of 18 completed reviews (22% Reasonable, 44% Limited, 6% No Assurance)
findings.quote: the Head of East Kent Audit Partnership concluded a REASONABLE ASSURANCE whilst noting that for the period following 31 March 2026. (post the year end date) much work has been undertaken, and the position is a continuously moving target.

findings.headline: Prior-year accounts received a disclaimed opinion due to evidence limitations
findings.detail: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts was completed and received a disclaimed opinion in February 2026, in line with the Government's backstop dates. Detailed reviews of the process and information have been undertaken, and dedicated resource has been added to the Accountancy team to support production of the 2025/26 statement. This suggests significant evidence or control gaps prevented the auditor from providing a standard opinion.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion indicates the auditor could not obtain sufficient evidence to form a conclusion on the accounts; lenders depend on audited financial statements to assess council financial position, and this undermines assurance.
findings.figures: 2024/25 Statement of Accounts; February 2026 disclaimed opinion
findings.quote: The 2024/25 Statement of Accounts was completed and received a disclaimed opinion in February 2026, in line with the Government's backstop dates.

findings.headline: HRA budget allocation for maintenance works remains uncertain as stock condition survey is only 90% complete
findings.detail: The 2026/27 HRA budget includes a £283k deficit allocation for 'catch up works, if required' from a stock condition survey that started in 2024/25 and remains only 90% complete. The final scope and cost of required maintenance works remain contingent on completion of the survey.
findings.matters: Final investment requirements for the HRA stock could exceed the £283k provision once the survey is complete, creating additional financial exposure not currently quantified
findings.figures: £283k deficit, survey c.90% complete
findings.quote: The HRA budget deficit of £283k is largely due to an allowance for catch up works, if required, following the stock condition survey and is not an on-going structural deficit.

findings.headline: Right to Buy legislative changes reducing capital receipts income
findings.detail: Section 7.2 notes 'Changes to Right to Buy (RTB) regulations have led to a reduction in RTB applications during 2025/26', reducing capital receipts. Assets available for sale are already limited.
findings.matters: Declining RTB receipts reduce capital funding available; combined with exhausted resources, limits ability to invest or respond to asset needs.
findings.figures: No quantified impact provided
findings.quote: Changes to 'Right to Buy' (RTB) regulations have led to a reduction in RTB applications during 2025/26.

findings.headline: General Fund forecasts only £32k surplus, leaving minimal buffer for cost pressures
findings.detail: Section 5.2 reports 2026/27 General Fund surplus of just £32k. Council acknowledges 'significant margin of uncertainty' from inflation and macroeconomic position; depends on £4m smoothing reserve to manage volatility (£1.28m already drawn down since 2022/23).
findings.matters: Minimal surplus provides no practical cushion for cost overruns or income shortfalls; council heavily dependent on reserve drawdown to manage normal budget volatility.
findings.figures: GF surplus £32k; smoothing reserve £4m; £1.28m drawn since 2022/23
findings.quote: The GF budget forecasts a surplus of £32k for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account viability depends on rigorous financial discipline for development programme
findings.detail: Section 6.5 states HRA is viable 'even with the underlying requirement to borrow to finance the housing development programme' but explicitly conditions this on 'rigorous financial discipline to ensure that the current investment programme is managed within existing and forecast resources'.
findings.matters: Conditional viability means housing sustainability is at risk if spending discipline slips or costs exceed forecast; lenders need visibility of HRA borrowing and cash flow.
findings.figures: HRA forecast £283k surplus 2026/27; rents increase 4.8%; typical 3-bed weekly rent £123.09
findings.quote: The HRA is viable now and in the medium term, even with the underlying requirement to borrow to finance the housing development programme. This relies on rigorous financial discipline

findings.headline: Capital resources virtually exhausted with current commitments
findings.detail: Section 7.2 establishes capital resources are now 'virtually exhausted if all current commitments are met and no new receipts or other sources are found'. Council faces significant challenge maintaining buildings without deterioration; ability of revenue budget to contribute to capital is 'very limited'.
findings.matters: Exhausted capital capacity forces reliance on borrowing for new investment; constrains ability to respond to asset deterioration or service needs.
findings.figures: Current capital programme £112.6m (fully funded); special revenue projects £19.9m (fully funded)
findings.quote: Capital resources are virtually exhausted if all current commitments are met and no new receipts or other sources are found

findings.headline: Bus Rapid Transit project flagged as major project of significant concern
findings.detail: Section 7.6-7.7 identifies Dover Fastrack as 'the current major project of significant concern'. The council is accountable body with grant funding; KCC appointed to deliver. Commercial confidentiality issues require excluding press/public from further discussion.
findings.matters: Infrastructure projects flagged as 'significant concern' indicate known risks; lenders need to understand what has gone wrong or is at risk.
findings.figures: Main contract value less than £20m
findings.quote: The current major project of significant concern is the Bus Rapid Transit project, also known as Dover Fastrack.

findings.headline: Council Tax base growth slowed to 1% in 2026/27; future growth assumed at 1% pa, below national averages.
findings.detail: The Council Tax base is forecast to increase by only 1% in 2026/27, from 42,119.72 to 42,551.70 Band D equivalents. This is impacted by the implementation of the revised Council Tax Support Scheme and growth in property numbers. Future growth is assumed at 1% pa. The Council Tax increase of 2.98% is within the Government's capping limits (3% or £5, whichever is greater), but DDC as a low-tax district cannot generate as much additional income from Council Tax increases as higher-tax areas.
findings.matters: Slow tax base growth limits the council's ability to grow revenue to match cost inflation. If base growth stays at 1% but cost inflation exceeds that, the council must find savings or reduce services. This is structural and not easily remedied.
findings.figures: Tax base growth 1% in 2026/27; 1% pa assumed for future years; Council Tax increase 2.98% (£6.57 on Band D)
findings.quote: The increase in the tax base from 42,119.72 Band D equivalent properties in 2025/26 to 42,551.70 equivalent properties in 2026/27, a rise of 1%, has been impacted due to a growth in property numbers, the proposed implementation of the revised Council Tax Support Scheme and an increase in the anticipated Collection rate in year.

findings.headline: Asset maintenance backlog is large and growing, with critical repairs needed at leisure centre, pier, museum, and heritage assets.
findings.detail: The Head of Property Assets confirms there are "sufficient resources to keep properties generally wind and water-tight, but it continues to be a challenge to maintain all buildings without deterioration." Significant expenditure is needed at: Tides Leisure Centre (new build in progress), Deal Pier (concrete structure with "enhanced rates of corrosion," main pylon repairs due 2026/27), Dover Museum (new roof and M&E replacement), Kearsney (bridge repairs, boardwalk), Roman Painted House (on Historic England Heritage at Risk Register). No single project cost is given, but the narrative suggests deferred maintenance is systemic.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance creates sudden, large costs that cannot be avoided indefinitely. A leisure centre replacement and pier structural repairs are not optional. These capital commitments compete with other priorities and with LGR transition costs.
findings.figures: Tides Leisure Centre: works due to commence early 2026; Deal Pier: pylon repairs due out early 2026, work in 2026/27; no individual cost figures given
findings.quote: There is a growing backlog of planned maintenance / project work required for DDC's "Operational Assets". Significant expenditure is needed at: Tides Leisure Centre – demolition of the old leisure pool hall is now complete with works on the main project and new build due to commence in early 2026. Deal Pier – a concrete clad metal structure in a maritime environment and therefore subject to enhanced rates of corrosion.

findings.headline: Capital resources are largely exhausted and future capital receipts from Right-to-Buy sales will drop significantly following legislative changes.
findings.detail: The council notes that "The current resources for funding capital and special revenue projects will be largely exhausted by the current programme." Right-to-Buy sales have increased in 2025/26 due to a recent change in legislation (which reduced the maximum cash discount from £102k to £38k), but this is temporary. Future RTB sales are "facing a reduction following the changes in regulations." This limits the council's ability to fund new capital projects without borrowing.
findings.matters: A council that cannot fund capital projects from reserves or receipts must borrow. Borrowing requires a revenue stream to service it. With homelessness costs rising, savings required in future years, and LGR costs unknown, new borrowing becomes riskier. The absence of capital flexibility is a constraint on the council's strategic options.
findings.figures: 28 RTB sales in 2025/26 (year to date); retained excess receipts forecast at £6.4m by year end; future receipts forecast to decline
findings.quote: Future capital receipts are expected to come mainly from on-going housing right to buy sales (which are facing a reduction following the changes in regulations) and one-off asset sales, so will not replenish capital funds and will not be sufficient to maintain the current level of activity in the future.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs increased by £537k in a single year; no end-date for the pressure is given.
findings.detail: Between the 2025/26 and 2026/27 budgets, homelessness and temporary accommodation costs increased by £537k. This is described as an "on-going service pressure" alongside Business Rates and Local Government Reorganisation but no mitigation plan or trajectory for reduction is outlined. Homelessness is listed as a significant budget risk.
findings.matters: A £537k cost increase in one year for homelessness suggests either rising need or rising unit costs (or both). Without a visible plan to address root causes or manage demand, this becomes an open-ended pressure that could grow faster than the overall budget.
findings.figures: £537k increase in homelessness temporary accommodation and associated costs between 2025/26 and 2026/27 budgets
findings.quote: Net increase in Homelessness temporary accommodation and associated costs 537

findings.headline: Significant savings of £1.6m in 2027/28 and £0.9m per year thereafter will be required; the council has not yet identified how these will be delivered.
findings.detail: The MTFP forecasts that on current assumptions the council will face a requirement to deliver savings and/or income generation of £1.6m in 2027/28, and a further £0.9m each year in 2028/29 and 2029/30. These figures are "subject to the impacts of the uncertainties and pressures and will be kept under review" and no specific saving plans are outlined. These pressures coincide with LGR implementation.
findings.matters: A council that has not identified how it will save £1.6m+ in two years, while facing simultaneous Local Government Reorganisation, is running on forecast and hope rather than concrete plans. This is a test of whether the council's financial management can keep pace with events.
findings.figures: £1.6m savings required 2027/28; £0.9m required 2028/29 and 2029/30
findings.quote: it is currently forecast that there will be a requirement to deliver savings and / or income generation in the region of £1.6m in 2027/28 and a further £0.9m in 2028/29 and 2029/30, as detailed in Annex 2. This value is subject to the impacts of the uncertainties and pressures and will be kept under review.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) funding of £1.4m has uncertain long-term basis and DEFRA has not explained how it is calculated.
findings.detail: EPR funding ($1.4m in 2025/26 and forecast to remain the same in 2026/27) offsets recycling service costs. However, despite government commitments that EPR would be "additional" funds, there are suggestions MHCLG may claw back elements of the settlement in future years. DEFRA has not been able to explain how the grant is calculated. As the packaging industry reacts to the tax, the grant is likely to erode over time.
findings.matters: A material income stream (£1.4m) rests on an unexplained calculation that may be withdrawn or reduced by government policy change. This is not a stable, controllable income source and represents a medium-term financial cliff.
findings.figures: £1.4m pa in 2025/26 and 2026/27; basis of calculation unexplained; long-term erosion expected
findings.quote: Despite apparent commitments that the EPR will be "additional" funds, there have been suggestions that MHCLG may use this to claw back elements of the settlement in future years. So, the basis of this grant for longer term financial planning is uncertain.

findings.headline: Port Health Authority funding for critical biosecurity checks remains unconfirmed by DEFRA; shortfall would force Dover to absorb cost from Council Tax.
findings.detail: DEFRA has not confirmed funding for Dover Port Health Authority's biosecurity activities in 2026/27, particularly checks on illegal meat entering Dover (African Swine Fever and other animal diseases). If funding is not secured, Dover must either severely limit DPHA activities (risking UK agricultural biosecurity) or cover the cost from local Council Tax at the expense of other services. The council currently assumes DPHA will be budget-neutral.
findings.matters: A central government function (port health) may be unfunded, forcing a local council to choose between a hidden subsidy or operational failure. This is a structural vulnerability in the council's budget and represents an unquantified contingent liability.
findings.figures: None given; currently assumed budget-neutral
findings.quote: DEFRA has not yet confirmed funding for Dover Port Health Authority's (DPHA) biosecurity activities in 2026/27, specifically for checks on illegal meat entering Dover (no checks are currently taking place at Coquelles). These checks are critical to mitigating significant and evolving animal health risks. While initially focused on African swine fever (ASF), the scope has expanded to include additional diseases in response to the changing animal health disease landscape within the EU. If adequate funding for 2026/27 is not secured, DDC would need to significantly limit its DPHA activities (with continuing high risk to UK agriculture biosecurity, ASF and FMD, food security, economic, and reputational risks) or meet some of the cost of DPHA activities itself, from local Council Tax, to the detriment of other services.

findings.headline: Business Rates baseline reset and 76% revaluation creates unprecedented complexity and appeal risk, with Channel Tunnel alone rising 195%.
findings.detail: The draft 2026 revaluation shows Dover's rateable value rising from £129m to £227m. The Channel Tunnel alone rises from £40m to £118m and is subject to appeal. The council only retains ~40% of Business Rates income but must fund 100% of refunds if appeals succeed. The safety net is set at 100% for 2026/27 but forecast to drop to 97% and 92.5% thereafter, meaning losses above those levels fall to the council. These changes mean the council bears full appeal risk on a volatile base.
findings.matters: If major properties successfully appeal their valuations, Dover loses revenue it has already planned to retain and budgeted to pay onwards to government. The absence of a national appeals pool means one major appeal can materially harm a single council's finances. The Channel Tunnel concentration is extreme.
findings.figures: Rateable value increases from £129.3m to £226.9m (76%); Channel Tunnel from £40m to £118m (195% increase, subject to appeal); current BR income £5.4m (24% of total financing)
findings.quote: Overall, the 2026 draft list shows an increase in Rateable Value for the Dover district of 76% from £128m to £226m. This doesn't necessarily mean a proportionate increase in the amount collectable, since many premises have small business or other relief... The increase also does not mean more retained by DDC, since the baseline is increased to offset the RV increase.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasts a £283k deficit in 2026/27, the first loss after years of surplus.
findings.detail: The HRA is expected to run a deficit rather than surplus for the coming year. This is driven by increased repairs and maintenance spend (£1m increase), temporary borrowing costs for housing development (£903k), and salary inflation (£648k), partially offset by rent increases (£1.18m from existing dwellings, £277k from new stock). The deficit will be covered from the Housing Initiatives Reserve, which is forecast to remain at £20m.
findings.matters: Persistent deficits would erode the HRA's financial resilience. A council that cannot cover housing operations from rent and existing reserves becomes dependent on borrowing or subsidy. This matters for debt service capability and housing investment plans.
findings.figures: £283k deficit; repairs and maintenance up £1m; new stock interest payable £903k; rent increases £1.18m from existing, £277k from new stock
findings.quote: The HRA forecasts a deficit for 2026/27 of £283k. The deficit will be financed by the Housing Initiatives Reserve (HIR). The HIR balance is forecast at £20m at the end of 2026/27.

findings.headline: Dover District Council will cease to exist on 1 April 2028 and finances must remain uncertain until Local Government Reorganisation structure is confirmed.
findings.detail: The council is planning for dissolution as part of a government-driven Local Government Reorganisation. The planned timeline means Dover has at least 2 more years of operation, but the structure of successor authorities, harmonisation of Council Tax and other charges, and costs of transition remain unknown. The S151 officers acknowledge this is "largely out of our control" but continue planning on the assumption of business-as-usual.
findings.matters: A council facing dissolution within 2 years may struggle to attract talent, maintain service standards, or deliver long-term projects. Lenders must understand both the immediate operational risk and the uncertainty over which authority will assume existing borrowing.
findings.figures: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Based on the proposed timescale for LGR from MHCLG, Dover District Council will cease to exist from 01 April 2028. With this in mind, there are at least 2 further years of Dover District Council and therefore this MTFP may stretch beyond the last year of DDC (subject to the Government timeline for LGR).

findings.headline: Income pressures across car parking, building control, and land charges; car parking below budget forecast
findings.detail: Car parking gross income is forecast £3.1m for 2025/26, below the original budget; 2026/27 budget holds flat at £3.1m. Building Control receipts are below forecast due to construction slowdown from cost-of-living impacts. Land charges income is in structural decline: budget reduced from £130k to £120k 'due to a steadily declining property market.'
findings.matters: Multiple income streams under pressure signal demand weakness in the district; a lender would want to understand sustainability of income forecasts, particularly car parking and development fees which are discretionary.
findings.figures: Car parking 2025/26 forecast £3.1m (below budget), held at £3.1m for 2026/27; Land charges £130k budget reduced to £120k
findings.quote: The 2025/26 gross income (before costs) for parking fees and penalty charge notices is currently forecast to be performing below the 2025/26 budget, totalling £3.1m. […] The original 2025/26 budget was set at £130k but the forecast has been reduced to £120k, due a steadily declining property market in the year.

findings.headline: Pension lump sum (backfunding) rises 35% to £1.84m on triennial valuation, though partially offset by rate reduction
findings.detail: The Kent County Council pension fund triennial valuation (March 2025, implemented April 2026) increases Dover's lump sum backfunding from £1.35m to £1.84m. The council notes that the current-service contribution rate falls from 20.2% to 16.6%, resulting in 'a minimal, favourable, impact' on total budget impact, but the lump sum increase itself is material.
findings.matters: Large pension contributions are a fixed cost that limits budget flexibility; a 35% increase signals actuarial assumptions about asset performance and longevity have shifted, affecting long-term affordability.
findings.figures: Backfunding lump sum increases from £1.35m to £1.84m; current-service rate 20.2% (2025/26) to 16.6% (2026/27)
findings.quote: As a result of the triennial valuation the back funding lump sum payment will be increased from £1.35m to £1.84m in 2026/27. […] The impact of the reduction in current contributions is approximately equal to the increase in the backfunding lump sum; therefore, the total of the changes has a minimal, favourable, impact on the budget figures.

findings.headline: MTFP forecasts structural deficits of £1.6–£3.4m in 2027–2030, requiring equivalent savings
findings.detail: The three-year revenue forecast (Annex 2) shows deficits of £1,585k (2027/28), £2,519k (2028/29), and £3,447k (2029/30). The council identifies 'target savings required' of £1,600k, £2,500k, and £3,400k for those years respectively—indicating the council's own awareness that savings plans equivalent to the deficits must land to keep the budget in balance.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know whether a council has identified credible savings plans to close forecast deficits; implicit reliance on unspecified future savings is a structural vulnerability.
findings.figures: Forecast deficits: 2027/28 £1,585k, 2028/29 £2,519k, 2029/30 £3,447k; Target savings required: £1,600k, £2,500k, £3,400k respectively
findings.quote: Estimated target savings required if current funding assumptions realised.

findings.headline: Homelessness costs forecast to grow beyond £1.9m as demand continues to rise
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation (after grant and Housing Benefit) costs Dover £1.9m in 2026/27. The council has identified this as a demand-led service driven by a national housing shortage, and explicitly forecasts continued increases. Mitigation steps (prevention, partnership working) are underway but the paper states 'homelessness pressures are expected to continue to increase.'
findings.matters: An explicitly growing cost with limited council control exposes the council to an open-ended budget pressure; a lender would want to know how this is funded if it continues rising.
findings.figures: £1.9m net costs to DDC from temporary accommodation in 2026/27
findings.quote: Homelessness is a demand led service. There is a national shortage of housing that has accrued over many years leading to the use of TA which creates a budget pressure. The net costs to DDC of TA (after grant funding and Housing Benefit income) in 2026/27 are estimated to be £1.9m. […] Nonetheless, homelessness pressures are expected to continue to increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Progress Update on External Audit Recs
findings.headline: Finance team restructuring underway to address control gaps, targeting completion by end of March 2026
findings.detail: The council has approved restructuring its finance team with a focus on system development and improving data accuracy at the source. The recruitment process for the new structure is underway and aims to improve the efficiency of processes and reduce transactions going to suspense accounts.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether councils have sufficient financial capacity and capability; a restructuring signals previous gaps but the proactive remediation is important to monitor.
findings.figures: New structure targeting completion by end of March 2026
findings.quote: Approval has been given to amend the team structure to provide a focus on system development and improvement, getting the data right at source and improving the efficiency of processes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Progress Update on External Audit Recs
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation and suspense account clearance remain incomplete with only Reasonable Assurance from internal audit
findings.detail: The council had significant audit findings on bank reconciliations and suspense accounts. Internal audit follow-up shows only Reasonable Assurance (6 of 8 recommendations implemented), up from No Assurance previously. Main outstanding items are clearance of suspense accounts and team resilience. The council is recruiting a new team structure focused on system development and data accuracy, aiming for completion by end of March 2026.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial control strength; incomplete bank reconciliations and suspense account management indicate governance weaknesses that affect financial reporting reliability and cash management.
findings.figures: Bank reconciliation: 6 of 8 recommendations implemented; Income: increased from No Assurance to Limited Assurance with 4 of 9 recommendations implemented
findings.quote: The main outstanding items from the audit relate to the clearance of the income suspense accounts and the development of resilience within the team.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Council subject to Local Government Reorganisation with replacement by new unitary authority expected by 2028
findings.detail: Dover will cease to exist as a separate authority when it is replaced by a new larger unitary authority by 2028 as part of the government's Local Government Reorganisation programme for Kent. The council is currently a coalition administration with no overall political control (changed from Labour-led in 2025). The auditor notes that resolving legacy governance issues promptly is important for facilitating planning for the successor unitary.
findings.matters: Pending local government reorganisation creates capacity risks and governance uncertainty during the transition period. Councils in LGR face distraction and resource constraints during the restructuring process, potentially delaying resolution of existing issues.
findings.figures: New unitary authority expected by 2028; council became coalition administration with no overall control in 2025
findings.quote: In the context of Local Government Re-organisation (LGR) in Kent, it will be important that legacy governance issues are resolved promptly to facilitate planning for the new unitary authorities.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Four Statutory Recommendations remain in place from January 2025, with governance issues not yet fully resolved
findings.detail: The auditor carried forward four statutory recommendations from January 2025: SR1 (bank reconciliations and suspense accounts), SR3 (governance oversight), and SR4 (system implementation arrangements) remain outstanding. SR2 (financial reporting) was closed but converted to a Key Recommendation. The auditor notes that although some progress has been made, 'the governance issues we identified in prior years are not yet fully resolved' and internal audit found only 'Limited Assurance' on internal controls.
findings.matters: Multiple outstanding statutory recommendations from the same year indicate systemic governance weaknesses and slow pace of improvement. Limited assurance from internal audit suggests pervasive control weaknesses across the organization.
findings.figures: 4 statutory recommendations; 3 remain unresolved; Internal Audit gave 'overall Limited Assurance' on internal controls; multiple recommendations outstanding since 2021-22
findings.quote: Ongoing significant weakness in arrangements identified in financial management and the production of financial performance information. Statutory Recommendations issued on 17 January 2025.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation completion is significantly delayed with March 2025 reconciliation not completed until July 2025
findings.detail: The council cannot demonstrate that bank reconciliations were completed in a timely manner throughout 2024-25. The March 2025 bank reconciliation, a critical financial control, was not completed until July 2025 — a four-month delay. This is a continuation of a multi-year Statutory Recommendation dating back to 2021-22.
findings.matters: Timely bank reconciliation is a fundamental financial control. A four-month delay indicates either resource constraints or control failures, and raises concerns about the completeness and accuracy of the cash position.
findings.figures: March 2025 bank reconciliation completed July 2025 (4-month delay); issue ongoing since 2021-22
findings.quote: We understand that following the implementation of the income management module in Tech-1 in December 2024, the Council experienced further issues and delays in the completion of bank reconciliations, with the March 2025 reconciliation not being completed until July 2025.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Council has not demonstrated appropriate focus and urgency in responding to audit recommendations
findings.detail: The auditor identifies a significant weakness in governance: management has rejected multiple external and internal audit recommendations and has sometimes lacked urgency in implementing accepted recommendations. Only 165 of 172 internal audit recommendations (96%) were accepted in 2024-25, but delivery has been slow. The auditor notes management response has sometimes been 'muted or non-receptive' and that the council must develop a culture that welcomes challenge and uses it to drive improvement.
findings.matters: A council that does not respond effectively to audit findings cannot be relied upon to address emerging financial or operational risks. This pattern suggests weak governance culture and management accountability.
findings.figures: 172 internal audit recommendations in 2024-25; 7 rejected (4%); multiple prior-year recommendations still outstanding or only partially implemented
findings.quote: the Council has not always demonstrated the level of focus and urgency towards audit recommendations which we would expect to see from working with other councils with significant challenges

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs created £1.278m budget overspend in 2024-25 and pressures continue into 2025-26
findings.detail: The deficit was primarily driven by temporary accommodation cost pressures, which exceeded budget by £1.278m in 2024-25. These pressures have continued and were built into the 2025-26 budget, indicating an ongoing structural pressure on the council's finances.
findings.matters: Persistent temporary accommodation pressures indicate growing housing stress and constrained local supply, a marker of councils facing demand-driven budget challenges that cannot easily be controlled.
findings.figures: £1.278m temporary accommodation overspend in 2024-25; pressures continuing into 2025-26
findings.quote: The deficit of £0.776m on 2024-25 outturn, primarily due to temporary accommodation cost pressures, was covered by the Council's Smoothing Reserve.

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: £2m of unidentified savings (approximately 10% of net expenditure) required over 4-year MTFP but work has only just begun
findings.detail: The council's Medium-Term Financial Plan requires £2m in savings over the 4-year period from 2025-26 to be balanced, representing a significant portion of annual net expenditure. However, these savings have not been identified. The auditor notes that work started on identifying them only in summer 2025. The council used the Smoothing Reserve to cover the 2024-25 deficit but plans not to use it going forward.
findings.matters: Unidentified savings represent a material planning risk. If the council cannot identify and deliver these savings, it will face a structural deficit requiring further reserve depletion or service cuts.
findings.figures: £2m savings required; £0.776m deficit in 2024-25 covered by Smoothing Reserve; savings represent circa 10% of Council's annual net expenditure
findings.quote: The medium-term challenge for the Council is significant as the MTFP indicates savings of £2m will be required in the 4-year period from 2025-26. These savings are yet to be fully identified but we note work started on long-term programme to identify them in summer 2025

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: New income system implementation in December 2024 created 4,807 erroneous transactions worth £457m posted to suspense accounts
findings.detail: The implementation of the new income management module caused system configuration errors that resulted in massive transaction errors. Despite improved project management arrangements, there were deficiencies in risk management, insufficient resilience and contingency planning, and inadequate testing before go-live. As of the report date, the council is still working to clear 1,464 transactions valued at £5.2m from suspense accounts.
findings.matters: System implementation failures indicate weak project governance and control, with the council unable to complete even basic financial controls (bank reconciliations) in a timely manner. This raises questions about financial management capability.
findings.figures: 4,807 transactions totalling £457m posted to suspense accounts; 1,464 transactions valued £5.2m still being cleared; March 2025 bank reconciliation not completed until July 2025
findings.quote: the system implementation was problematic and created additional entries into the suspense accounts (4,807 transactions valuing £457m), increasing the balances significantly for the period December 2024 to May 2025. At the time of this report work is still ongoing to clear the suspense accounts (1,464 transactions, value £5.2m).

findings.paper_title: Auditor's Annual Report 2024-25 Dover District Council_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Audit opinion will be disclaimed for the second consecutive year due to failure to produce Code-compliant financial statements
findings.detail: The council has not delivered financial statements that comply with the Code of Practice on Local Authority Accounting for 2023-24 or 2024-25. Key disclosures are missing or incomplete, including investment property valuations, financial instruments disclosures, and IFRS 16 implementation. The auditor states that without the backstop disclaimer, they would be unable to issue unqualified opinions for either year.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means there is no independent assurance over the council's financial position, making it impossible for lenders or senior finance officers to rely on the published accounts.
findings.figures: 2023-24 and 2024-25 financial statements subject to disclaimed audit opinions; 2020-21, 2021-22, 2022-23 also subject to disclaimed opinions
findings.quote: Had a backstop disclaimed opinion not been required, due to prior years' accounts being subject to a disclaimed opinion, we would not have been able to issue unqualified opinions for 2023-24 or 2024-25, due to the low level of Code compliance.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: No assurance over opening balances or closing reserves balance due to prior year disclaimed opinions.
findings.detail: Following disclaimed opinions in prior years, auditors have no assurance over opening balances for 2024-25 and no assurance over the closing reserves balance due to uncertainty over opening positions. This severely limits the scope of audit work and auditors' ability to verify year-end financial position.
findings.matters: Without assurance on opening balances or reserves, lenders cannot rely on the reported financial position or movement in reserves as a control indicator or indicator of financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Opening balances and closing reserves both subject to no assurance
findings.quote: we have no assurance over the opening balances for the 2024-25 financial statements; and we have no assurance over the closing reserves balance, also due to the uncertainty over their opening positions.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Council dwellings valuations based on unverified 2021 base valuation; no assurance over opening balance.
findings.detail: The 2024-25 council dwellings valuation is based on a full Beacon valuation carried out in 2021. Auditors have no assurance over this 2021 opening balance as management cannot demonstrate that the original 2021 valuation was RICS-compliant. The auditor's expert recommended a full refresh of the Beacon valuation at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Council dwellings represent a material asset. An unverified opening valuation cascades uncertainty through the year-end balance and prevents auditors from drawing conclusions on asset reliability.
findings.figures: 2021 base valuation; auditor's expert recommendation for full refresh at March 2026
findings.quote: However, the 2025 valuations are based on the full Beacon valuation carried out in 2021. We have no assurance over the 2021 valuation, and hence the opening balance for 2024-25, as management is unable to demonstrate that the original 2021 valuation was RICS compliant.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Material property assets (c.20% of land & buildings) held at valuations not verified as RICS-compliant.
findings.detail: Approximately 20% of the Authority's land and buildings estate was revalued in-year, creating a material balance of assets for which auditors are unable to conclude whether valuations are RICS-compliant and therefore Code-compliant. This leaves a risk of material misstatement in the balance sheet.
findings.matters: Asset valuations are a major component of the balance sheet. Inability to verify RICS compliance creates material uncertainty over reported asset values and financial position.
findings.figures: c.20% of land & buildings revalued in-year; auditors unable to conclude RICS compliance
findings.quote: Management revalued circa 20% of its land & buildings and all investment properties at 31 March 2025, meaning a material balance of assets is held in the accounts under valuations not considered to be RICS and therefore Code compliant and could be materially misstated.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in financial sustainability and governance arrangements.
findings.detail: The Value for Money assessment concluded that significant weaknesses exist in the Authority's arrangements for financial sustainability and governance. Auditors are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.
findings.matters: A qualified VFM conclusion signals systemic weaknesses in financial management and governance oversight, directly affecting credit risk assessment.
findings.figures: Identified in separate 2024-25 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Authority's arrangements in the areas of financial sustainability and governance, and so are not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Council has not implemented IFRS 16 leases standard, which became mandatory from 1 April 2024.
findings.detail: The Authority did not complete the assessment required to implement IFRS 16 accounting for leases, which took effect from 1 April 2024. Management performed a review of leased assets but did not perform an assessment of the car leasing scheme. Auditors could not complete audit work in this area.
findings.matters: Non-implementation of mandatory accounting standards is a regulatory compliance failure. Lenders rely on audited accounts prepared under the Code of Practice; omitting a material standard represents a departure from requirements.
findings.figures: Effective from 1 April 2024; auditors issued no opinion in this area
findings.quote: The Authority has not taken appropriate steps to implement IFRS 16, we therefore did not complete work in this area. Management has committed to performing the assessment for IFRS 16, for it to be included in the 2025-26 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Grant income adjustments of £6.3m identified; auditors unable to confirm correct classification of £0.7m homelessness grant.
findings.detail: Testing of grant income identified multiple errors. A prior period adjustment of £2.3m for National Lottery Heritage Fund income was recorded. Two adjustments totalling £4.1m were made to 2024-25 accounts (Local Authority Housing Fund £1.9m, National Lottery Heritage Fund £2.2m). An unadjusted misstatement of £0.7m relating to a Homelessness Grant remains due to classification uncertainty.
findings.matters: Grant income errors indicate control gaps in the revenue recognition process. Unresolved misstatements of this size suggest income balances may not be fully reliable.
findings.figures: £2.3m prior period adjustment; £1.9m + £2.2m current year adjustments; £0.7m unadjusted misstatement
findings.quote: Sample testing of grant income identified a number of errors. We also identified two adjustments to the 2024-25 financial statements relating to the Local Authority Housing Fund (£1.9m); and National Lottery Heritage Fund income (£2.2m). Furthermore, we identified an unadjusted misstatement with regard to a Homelessness Grant (£0.7m) where we were unable to confirm the correct classification of income

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Bank reconciliations were not completed timely during 2024-25, repeating a prior-year control failure.
findings.detail: Bank reconciliations, a foundational financial control, were not completed on a timely basis during the year ended 31 March 2025. The delay followed implementation of the income management module in December 2024, which created significant difficulties. This repeats the same finding from 2023-24 and remains subject to a prior statutory recommendation.
findings.matters: Untimely bank reconciliations mean income, expenditure and cash balances may not be correctly recorded. This control failure directly undermines revenue and cash assurance and perpetuates audit limitations.
findings.figures: Reconciliation at 31 March 2025 not completed until July 2025; recurring finding from 2023-24
findings.quote: Following the implementation of the income management module on TechOne in December 2024, the finance team encountered significant difficulties in preparing and agreeing the reconciliations. The bank reconciliation is a key foundational control in any finance system.

findings.paper_title: Dover District Council 2024-25 Audit Findings Report_GC 12 February 2026
findings.headline: Auditors will disclaim opinion on 2024-25 financial statements due to incomplete audit work.
findings.detail: The auditors explicitly state they are unable to form an opinion on the 2024-25 financial statements and will issue a disclaimed audit opinion. This follows multiple years of disclaimed opinions due to backstop legislation. The inability to obtain assurance on opening balances and closing reserves is a primary driver.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means audited accounts provide no assurance to lenders on the reliability of the financial position reported. This is a material credit indicator.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; prior year (2023-24) also disclaimed
findings.quote: we will be unable to form an opinion on the 2024-25 financial statements. Our anticipated financial statements audit report opinion will be a disclaimed audit opinion

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing nearly tripled from £37m to £88m, driven by housing development projects being funded through borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's short-term inter-authority borrowing increased materially from £37m at the start of 2025/26 to £88m by end September 2025. This increase is explicitly attributed to housing development projects being funded through borrowing alongside cash flow fluctuations. Meanwhile, the investment portfolio remained stable at £46.143m, supported by this short-term borrowing strategy.
findings.matters: A 138% increase in short-term borrowing represents a material shift in the council's debt profile and leverage. Using short-term funding to finance longer-term housing development projects creates refinancing risk, and a lender would want to understand the development timeline, expected cash generation, and the council's plan to repay or refinance this borrowing.
findings.figures: Short-term borrowing: £37m to £88m; long-term investments: £46.143m
findings.quote: Short term cashflow borrowing increased from £37m to £88m due to housing development projects being funded through borrowing and fluctuations in the cash flow requirements.

news_drafts.headline: Council Tax and Business Rates collection below target; cost-of-living distress and court enforcement delays threaten further deterioration
news_drafts.lead: Collection rates below target reduce available cash and may require bad debt provision increases. Court enforcement constraints coupled with cost-of-living pressures indicate collection challenges may be structural rather than temporary.

news_drafts.headline: HRA tenant rent arrears deteriorating: up to 1.49% of annual rental income from 1.15% year-on-year
news_drafts.lead: Deteriorating rent collection indicates tenant financial stress and reduces reliable HRA income. This compounds existing deficits and could necessitate higher bad debt provisions, further pressuring service sustainability.

news_drafts.headline: HRA stock condition survey (91.5% complete) may identify additional capital investment requirements above budget
news_drafts.lead: Unquantified cost pressures emerging on a service already running deficits represents material financial uncertainty. Completion of this survey could reveal substantial additional needs, further straining finances.
